{"self_assessment": "**Impact:** I put the fish sketch on the pad early, so the table could start tracing without waiting. I also pushed us to commit to one plan. The body and both tail fins are standing and connected to the start, so the fall should read as a fish facing right. It is not clean, though. By my count only about 131 of 189 standing dominoes were connected. The back edge of the tail and the bottom corner were still messy at the end, and several pale pieces near the tail won't fall. I think the outline is recognizable, but I can't promise it. My own hands-on contribution was small: a few dominoes on the tail's back edge, not a whole stroke.

**Execution:** The sketch gave us a workable layout where the strokes branched off the nose and flowed toward the tail. I should have flagged sooner that the tail needed more hands. The fins only started around the halfway mark, which is why the back edge was still unresolved with two minutes left. I also said at one point that I'd take the top tail edge, but Maya had it covered. That was duplicated effort. When I told you the start 'carries almost all of it', I was a bit more upbeat than the evidence supported. The accurate version is that the body and fins carry and the back edge and corner are uncertain.

**Collaboration:** I kept everyone informed and tried to deconflict hands, for example by backing off the bottom corner so Tom could bridge it without bumping anyone. I stopped working when we were crowding each other. The team was good-natured and kept stepping on each other's announcements, and I added to that chatter more than I needed to.

**Leadership:** I helped settle the plan and divided the strokes. I stayed calm as time ran down, and I called for hands-off in the last two minutes so nobody knocked anything over. Leo and Tom drove much of the actual building, and I could have directed people to the tail earlier rather than reassuring the table."}
